## The bag's second half

[Section 1](01-trade-history.qmd) explained why a cheap supermarket bag *exists* after silver, war, and plant transfer. This lesson asks what an **estate** does once Chinese monopoly leaf is no longer the only farm—who clears the jungle, who picks the flush, and how that commodity form reaches a British cupboard.

Hold two pictures. In one, Fortune's packing cases and Assam identification finish the road *to* the monopoly break. In the other, cleared forest, migrant labor schedules, and a late-nineteenth-century Britain that no longer depends on Canton chests. Chemistry still lives in [Chapter 1](../module-01/index.qmd). Aisle words still live in [Tea basics](../../tea-basics.qmd). This sitting owns the **aftershock**—land, labor, marketing, and the estate form that makes the bag historically cheap.

We thinned Section 1's aftershock paragraphs on purpose so the estate story is not told twice.
:::

## From plant transfer to industrial crop

Botany and politics opened the door. Estates walked through it.

Assam tea was identified and validated decades before Fortune's China missions; Fortune layered Chinese *sinensis* cultivars, makers, and know-how onto an industry already underway—that hinge lives in Section 1.[^1][^2] What followed was not a few experimental plots. It was a commercial vehicle, then a landscape of gardens: frontier clearance, imported and managed labor, and commodity schedules that could feed a mass market.[^3][^5]

On **12 February 1839**, merchants met in London at 6 Great Winchester Street and formed a Provisional Committee to pursue Assam tea cultivation and manufacture as private enterprise—after the East India Company's experimental gardens had already shown the plant could work.[^5] The **Assam Company** that grew from that meeting is the standard first commercial tea company for Assam gardens: the bridge from government experiment to shareholder estate. The named timeline (formation, early Chinese skilled recruits, then the migrant-labor turn) lives in the foldout below; the open story only needs the hinge—once Chinese monopoly leaf was optional, capital organized the garden.[^5][^6]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Assam Company & early garden boom (named timeline)"}
| Beat | What the sources support | Fence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **12 Feb 1839** | London merchants meet at 6 Great Winchester Street; Provisional Committee formed to pursue Assam tea as private enterprise after EIC experiments[^5] | Company-history narrative (Antrobus)—not a claim that no leaf was grown before |
| **First commercial vehicle** | Assam Company is the standard early commercial firm for Assam gardens[^5][^6] | Prefer Antrobus / Sharma over broker marketing sites |
| **Chinese skilled recruits** | Early attempts to import Chinese makers/workers largely abandoned by the **1860s** (death, desertion, cost); industry shifts toward cheaper, controlled migrant labor[^6] | Do not invent wage or mortality series on this page |

| **Acreage grants** | Waste Land Rules grant tallies (e.g. early land-admin figures) | **Skipped**—Assam.gov land-admin page was unavailable at research time; no invented acres |

## Gardens that remake a frontier

Picture Upper Assam not as a tidy English farm but as jungle cleared for rows: forest cut, land scheduled to a flush calendar, leaf moving on steamer and later rail toward a British market that wanted volume more than craft romance.[^1][^3] An estate is a timetable as much as a place—when the flush comes, leaf must be plucked, withered, and fired on schedule, then graded for chests that can travel. That commodity rhythm is what turns a frontier garden into something a counting house can price.

Kew's public history is blunt about the human and animal cost of clearance—coolies and elephants in the making of gardens—and about **Maniram Datta Barua**, who had first told Robert Bruce about Assam leaf, being executed after the 1857 uprising.[^1] The open story keeps those names as cost notes, not as a homemade body count: Kew supplies the readable trail; we do not invent mortality percentages beside it.

Sharma's *Empire's Garden* is the scholarly spine for how the British remade a jungle-laden frontier into cultivated estates, then reshaped the region's social landscape through migrant settlement.[^3] Duke University Press summarizes her argument as the settlement of more than one million migrants changing Assam's social landscape—we treat that as the publisher's framing of Sharma's thesis, not a fresh census counted on this page.[^3] That is history of land and people—not a spreadsheet of colonial profit shares invented here. Darjeeling appears in Section 1's four-era hinge as another late-nineteenth-century Raj garden name; this sitting keeps Assam as the spine and leaves Darjeeling as a pointer unless a dedicated monograph is added later.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Assam / Darjeeling estate sketch (named trails only)"}
| Place / trail | What the sources support | Fence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Assam** | Engineered plantation landscape; indentured / migrant labor; racialized "coolie" construction; frontier clearance (Sharma)[^3][^6] | Do not invent acreage grants or wage series here |

:::

## Who works the garden

Planters and officials did not treat Assamese peasants as a ready workforce. By the **1850s**, labor was already the chief obstacle; the industry leaned on a racialized ideology of "lazy natives" and turned toward **displaced migrants** from other parts of British India.[^6][^3] The garden needed hands on a schedule the planters claimed locals would not keep—so the empire moved people instead of rewriting the timetable.

From the **1860s until the 1920s**, Assam plantations recruited laborers under a **penal and indentured** regime. Beginning with the **Transport of Native Labourers Act, 1863**, the colonial state passed laws that facilitated recruitment and control.[^6] Men, women, and children were sent from **Central India**—Chotanagpur laborers especially prized by the late nineteenth century—via steamers, roads, and later railways into Upper Assam's jungles and gardens.[^6] Sharma cites a contemporary order-of-magnitude estimate of roughly **700,000–750,000** recruits to Assam tea between **1870 and 1900**, about **250,000** of them from Chotanagpur—and she sets that estimate beside *Times* propaganda about "prosperity and peace," not as proof that indenture was welfare.[^6] The foldout keeps the attribution and the fence; the open story only needs the scale of the migration.

Teach the word **"coolie"** carefully: historically it named low-rung Indian Ocean wage labor; under Assam recruitment it gained a **specific racial attribution** tied to Central Indian / Chotanagpur migrants and planter rankings of who supposedly suited estate work. Planters contrasted supposedly "docile" migrant hill laborers with locals cast as lazy or opium-sodden—an ideological labor strategy, not a neutral ethnography.[^6] Sharma's larger argument is that this racialized construction of the tea laborer later fed Assamese elite identity politics—burden pushed onto tribals and migrant laborers. One foldout sentence is enough; this is not a nationalism lesson.[^3][^6]

Indenture made the industry largely independent of local labor, but locals still appear in niches (for example Kachari seasonal workers); after the 1861 Phulaguri context, planter views of Kachari labor soured further.[^6] Early Chinese skilled recruits, tried when the gardens still hoped for craft know-how from China, had largely been abandoned by the 1860s—too costly, too many deaths and desertions, relative to the controlled migrant stream that followed.[^6]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: migrants, contracts, and the coolie category (Sharma)"}
| Beat | Claim the sources support | Fence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Why migrants** | Officials/planters stigmatized Assamese peasants as "lazy natives"; by the 1850s labor was the chief obstacle; industry relied on racialized, displaced migrants[^6][^3] | Ideology, not ethnography |
| **Regime window** | **1860s–1920s**: Assam plantations recruit via a penal and indentured regime[^6] | Do not invent wage rates or passage mortality % |
| **Legal hinge** | **Transport of Native Labourers Act, 1863** begins a run of laws facilitating recruitment and control[^6] | Cite Sharma; do not paraphrase as "workers chose freely" |

## Cheap cup, honest fence

By about **1890**, Kew's public history says India supplied roughly **90%** of Britain's domestic tea market—the readable market trail for why a British cupboard no longer needed Canton chests the way it once did.[^1] The grocery bag is historically cheap partly because someone else's garden became an estate, and because that estate was staffed and scheduled for volume. Production alone does not finish the story: someone still had to persuade drinkers that empire leaf belonged in the everyday cup.

None of that licenses a slogan like "tea alone caused empire" or a homemade re-estimate of who kept plantation profits. Kew's page also says India was "only allowed to keep 15 percent of plantation profits"—we treat that as **Kew's narrative phrasing**, not an independently re-audited ledger on this site.[^1] Prefer Sharma for labor depth; keep Kew for the readable market-and-cost trail; keep Antrobus for the company-formation hinge.[^3][^5][^6]

Your grocery bag is cheap partly because someone else's garden became an estate. That sentence is history. It is not a morality play with invented villains, and it is not Chapter 1's Assam-versus-*sinensis* tasting lesson.

Assam is the spine. Another empire garden—Ceylon (today's Sri Lanka)—switched from coffee to tea when rust hit; the dated beats stay in the foldout.[^4] And empire leaf still needed buyers: planters sold "British" tea against an older preference for China leaf—marketing is part of why the cheap bag becomes everyday.[^7]

::: {.callout-caution title="Honesty fence"}
- Refuse re-estimating colonial profit shares from this page.
- Refuse "tea alone caused…" claims already fenced in Section 1.
- Kew's ~1890 / ~90% Britain-market line, human-cost notes, and **"15% of plantation profits"** line are **Kew narrative**—context for the cheap bag, not a new econometric model.[^1]
- Do not quote planter or *Times* praise of indenture as factual welfare.[^6]
- Do not invent wage rates, passage mortality, or Waste Land grant acreage series.
- Chemistry of the cup still lives in Chapter 1; shopping labels live in Tea basics.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: Ceylon — coffee rust → tea (Taylor / Loolecondera)"}
McCarthy and Devine's *Tea and Empire* reconstructs James Taylor's Victorian planter life from letters and plantation evidence. Chapters include **"The rise and fall of 'King Coffee'"** and **"Transition to tea"**—and the book flags the dark side of planting (violence, oppression), not only celebration.[^4]

**Popular companion dates** (foldout color; attribute to industry timelines, not as a second primary ledger):[^4]

| Beat | Companion narrative |
| --- | --- |
| **1852** | Taylor arrives in Ceylon |
| Mid-**1860s** | Early Loolecondera tea plantings |
| Often narrated **~1867** | First commercial field story in public Ceylon-tea timelines |
| **~1869** onward | Coffee rust first signs; coffee collapse over the following decade(s) |

**Why it belongs here:** another estate form after monopoly China leaf—commodity rescue through replanting, with labor and land costs attached.  
**Why it stays a foldout:** Assam (Sharma + Kew + Antrobus) already carries the open-story aftershock; Ceylon deepens without stealing the plot.  
**Fence:** no exact acres or export pounds on this page; refuse "father of Ceylon tea" hagiography without noting that McCarthy & Devine also emphasize public scandal around Taylor's dismissal and death.[^4]
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: selling the empire cup (Rappaport)"}
Indian plantation tea did **not** automatically win British cups. Rappaport's *A Thirst for Empire* frames a significant British market for Indian teas from the **1880s**; by the **1890s**, Britons (and, in her framing, Irish and Australian drinkers too) were primarily drinking empire produce.[^7]

How was that preference taught?

- Planters and promoters sold Indian tea via **anti-Chinese adulteration fear**, and as modern / pure / patriotic / "British."[^7]
- Planters and associations (for example the Indian Tea Association in the late nineteenth century) pioneered large **cooperative publicity**—marketing is part of why the cheap bag becomes everyday.[^7]
- The industry was on "sure footing" only by the **late 1870s**, after earlier Assam errors and resistance—rhymes with Sharma's labor timeline without retelling Section 1's Fortune plot.[^7][^6]

**Chapter pointers** (jobs verified via TOC + introduction—not page-mined tallies):[^7]

| Rappaport chapter | Use on this section |
| --- | --- |
| Ch. 3 "A Little Opium, Sweet Words, and Cheap Guns" | Foldout pointer only—**Section 1 still owns the Opium War narrative**; here only "planting a global industry in Assam" as production aftershock |
| Ch. 5 "Industry and Empire" | Commodity-industry framing |
| Ch. 6 "The Planter Abroad" | Planters seeking consumers beyond the estate |
| Ch. 8 "Tea Revives the World" | Advertising slogan / publicity culture |

**Fence:** no Lipton founding myths, African tea percentages, or WWII anecdotes as open-story core. Cite Rappaport's verified intro framing and chapter jobs only.[^7]
:::

## Handoff

Chemistry still explains what is in the cup ([Chapter 1 · Plants](../module-01/01-plants.qmd)). Processing factories explain how leaf becomes grade ([Chapter 1 · Processing](../module-01/02-processing.qmd)). Tea basics still owns aisle words for strong black and bag. The next history section asks how *people script* the drink regionally—Chaoshan tables, Taiwan tea art, Hong Kong milk-tea counters—not how empires priced the leaf.

::: {.callout-tip title="You can stop here"}
- After the monopoly break, the Assam Company and Assam-style estates remade land and labor into a mass commodity.
- Indenture (1860s–1920s) and the racialized "coolie" category are labor history—teach the category; do not revive the slur.
- Kew's ~1890 Britain-market trail helps explain the cheap bag—with a human-cost fence and Kew's own "15% profits" phrasing left as Kew narrative.
- Sharma is the longer Assam land/labor trail; Antrobus names the company hinge; Rappaport covers selling empire tea; Ceylon's coffee→tea switch is optional depth.
- Next: living regional scripts—not lab ritual psychology (that is Chapter 4).
:::
